newsitem.title: USA: Police launch manhunt for two Texas separatists.
newsitem.headline: Police launch manhunt for two Texas separatists.

text.p: Police scoured a remote west Texas mountain range on Sunday for two escaped armed separatists a day after their group peacefully surrendered at the end of a week-long siege.
Helicopters, at least 20 bloodhounds and two teams of troopers on horseback searched throughout the night for the two men, identified as Richard Keyes and Mike Matson.

The two men, both in their early 20s, walked away from the Republic of Texas mountain compound when the separatist group's leader Richard McLaren, his wife and three others put down their guns and surrendered to police forces over a number of hours on Saturday.
Police saw Keyes and Matson escape into the Davis Mountains at around midday on Saturday but did not begin searching for them until four hours later, once the other Republic members had given up.

Officials said the two men were dressed in camouflage and armed with an assault rifle, a deer-hunting rifle and a 9mm pistol, but rejected suggestions they had moved too slowly and said Keyes and Matson did not pose a serious threat.
"They are armed but there is no general public around them. They are out there with the deer and mountain lions," Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox said.

He said police did not close in on the two men immediately because they did not want to jeopardise the on-going, delicate negotiations which eventually brought the surrender of McLaren and his other followers.

Cox said the quantity of explosives and firearms found inside the Republic's dilapidated compound demonstrated that ending the siege was more important than immediately pursuing and capturing the two escapees.
Twenty-four pipe bombs and about 10 gas tanks which could have been exploded were found inside, along with 10 long firearms and between 500 and 700 rounds of ammunition.
"It has gone from a crisis situation to a fairly routine manhunt," Cox told reporters.

McLaren and his other followers, who claim Texas is an independent nation, had vowed to defend their "embassy" compound to the death, but surrendered when scores of police surrounded them and prepared to move in.

They were taken to Presidio County Jail in nearby Marfa, Texas, and arraigned on Saturday night. McLaren was jailed without bond and faces state felony charges tied to the kidnapping of two neighbours at the start of the standoff last Sunday, as well as federal contempt of court charges.
His wife Evelyn and the three other Republic members -- Richard "White Eagle" Otto, Karen and Gregg Paulson and Robert Schedit -- were each held on $500,000 bond.
The McLarens spent Saturday night in the same jail cell, a privilege negotiated during the final hours of the siege.

All the prisoners and one of the two escapees could face between five years and 99 years in prison for the state felony charges. Matson faces no charges and police said they did not understand why he chose to run away.

McLaren had been holed up inside his compound for four months after an arrest warrant was issued against him on contempt charges, but the situation turned dangerous when police arrested a Republic member last Sunday and McLaren retaliated by ordering the kidnapping of two neighbours. They were released 12 hours later in a prisoner exchange.

McLaren finally agreed to turn himself in when Texas Rangers signed off on a "cease-fire agreement", which included recognition of the Republic of Texas and an assurance that McLaren will be given the opportunity to argue before a federal judge in Washington D.C. that there should be a referendum on the issue of Texas independence.
It also allows the Republic to fly its flag -- a lone yellow star on a blue field -- over the west Texas "embassy".
